primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Blau syndrome due to NOD2 pathogenic variants
mechanism: NOD2 is a cytosolic pattern-recognition receptor whose canonical bacterial ligand is muramyl dipeptide, a peptidoglycan component. Pathogenic NOD2 variants cause Blau syndrome, an early-onset granulomatous autoinflammatory syndrome affecting skin, joints, and eyes.
vignette: A 3-year-old boy has a persistent papular rash, boggy symmetric polyarthritis, and recurrent anterior uveitis. Skin biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. His mother had a similar illness in early childhood. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous pathogenic variant in NOD2.
lead: The normal protein encoded by the affected gene directly recognizes which of the following microbial products?
correct: Muramyl dipeptide derived from bacterial peptidoglycan
distractors: Lipopolysaccharide from the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria
Bacterial flagellin in the extracellular space
distractor_notes: Cell-surface/endosomal TLR4 is the canonical receptor for lipopolysaccharide; NOD2 instead detects a peptidoglycan-derived muramyl dipeptide in the cytosol.
TLR3 is a major sensor of double-stranded RNA; this is not the canonical NOD2 ligand.
TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG-rich DNA in endosomes; it is not the ligand-recognition function of NOD2.
TLR5 senses extracellular bacterial flagellin, whereas NOD2 recognizes cytosolic muramyl dipeptide.
key_expl: Blau syndrome is a NOD2-related granulomatous autoinflammatory disease characterized by early skin, joint, and ocular inflammation. NOD2 is an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor whose canonical ligand is muramyl dipeptide, a conserved component of bacterial peptidoglycan.
objective: Identify muramyl dipeptide as the canonical bacterial ligand sensed by the intracellular NOD2 receptor implicated in Blau syndrome.
